title: Momentum-Orthogonal Projection Tests Whether Optimizer-State Geometry Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization
method:
The core of this study is the Momentum-Orthogonal Projection (MOP) operator, applied as a post-step modification to the target parameter tensor. The hypothesis posits that breaking alignment between the weights and the accumulated gradient history (stored in the momentum buffer) may improve generalization. The operator is applied only in the intervention arm; in the control arm, it does nothing. Both arms share identical initialization, data ordering, hyperparameters, and training loop, differing only in this single post-step modification.

The operator modifies the target parameter tensor W by subtracting its projection onto the optimizer's momentum buffer M, row-wise. This ensures W becomes orthogonal to M on rows where M has non-negligible norm. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent. The scope is row-wise, applied after the optimizer step of every optimization step. The ordering is parallel across rows. Numerical safeguards include an epsilon of 1e-12 on the denominator and skipping rows if the M norm is zero.

The algorithm proceeds as follows: receive target parameter tensor W, optimizer momentum buffer M, and condition flag. If the condition flag equals 'control', terminate without modifying W. Compute row-wise squared norms of M. Create a mask for valid rows where the norm exceeds 1e-12. If no valid rows exist, terminate. Compute row-wise dot products between W and M. Compute projection scalars alpha as the dot product divided by the norm squared plus epsilon. Broadcast alpha to match W shape. Compute the projection update delta as alpha expanded times M. Apply the orthogonal projection by subtracting delta from W on valid rows in-place. Return. The following invariants hold throughout: W row norm decreases or stays same, and W becomes orthogonal to M on valid rows.

The control arm is defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs. One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

This operator expression is the right test of the hypothesis because it directly manipulates the geometric relationship between weights and momentum without altering the loss landscape. The registered comparator holds fixed the training objective, data ordering, and initialization, isolating the effect of the post-step projection. Mechanistic rationales for why this might improve generalization are hypotheses, not measured findings; the experiment measures only held-out classification accuracy.

Operator specification. MomentumOrthogonalProjection is applied to blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight. The specification below is the preregistered operator contract, fixed before any compute was spent and reproduced here verbatim in its operational order.

- Scope: row.
- Applied: the operator is invoked after the optimizer step of every optimization step: the operator modifies the parameters or optimizer state the standard update just produced, so the modification persists into subsequent steps and into the evaluated weights..
- Ordering: parallel across rows.
- Normalisation: none.
- Numerical safeguards: epsilon 1e-12 on denominator; skip if M norm zero.

Algorithm 1 gives the operator in full.

1. Receive target parameter tensor W.
2. Receive optimizer momentum buffer M.
3. Receive condition flag.
4. If condition flag equals 'control', terminate without modifying W.
5. Compute row-wise squared norms of M: norm_M_sq = sum(M * M, dim=1).
6. Create mask valid_rows = (norm_M_sq > 1e-12).
7. If no valid_rows exist, terminate without modifying W.
8. Compute row-wise dot products: dot = sum(W * M, dim=1).
9. Compute projection scalars: alpha = dot / (norm_M_sq + 1e-12).
10. Broadcast alpha to match W shape: alpha_expanded = alpha.unsqueeze(1).
11. Compute projection update: delta = alpha_expanded * M.
12. Apply orthogonal projection: W[valid_rows, :] = W[valid_rows, :] - delta[valid_rows, :].
13. Ensure W modification is in-place.
14. Return.

The following invariants hold throughout:
- W row norm decreases or stays same
- W becomes orthogonal to M on valid rows

Control arm. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (post step). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. If the condition the harness passes in is a control condition, return here: add no term to the training objective, and leave the registered target parameter and that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer exactly as received. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study.

results:
We walk through the evidence for the primary and confirmatory-replication cohorts separately. In the primary cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, we report each metric's mean with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval. On held-out classification accuracy, the proposed condition achieved a mean of 0.8951 (95% CI [0.8906, 0.8988]), while the baseline achieved 0.9068 (95% CI [0.9034, 0.9099]). The first negative control achieved 0.8898 (95% CI [0.8864, 0.8933]). Figure 1 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar; the axis starts at zero, so the bar lengths are comparable. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline. The dashed line marks the baseline mean, as an ordering reference only.

The paired contrast in the hypothesised direction for the proposed condition versus the baseline worsened accuracy by 0.01171 (95% CI [-0.01744, -0.00664], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-0.63). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. However, the interval lies entirely below zero and below the worthwhile margin. Figure 2 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the primary cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Zero marks no directional effect. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold. Support requires the lower confidence bound to exceed it. The 43 individual paired differences are plotted behind the interval at their exact values. The preregistered decision was that the direction was refuted.

In the confirmatory replication cohort, across 3 conditions and 43 seeds, the proposed condition achieved a mean of 0.8906 (95% CI [0.8866, 0.8947]), while the baseline achieved 0.9081 (95% CI [0.9043, 0.9118]). The first negative control achieved 0.8868 (95% CI [0.8822, 0.8913]). Figure 4 displays the mean held-out classification accuracy for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Bars are means over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The point estimate is printed above each bar. The figure shows the proposed condition against the baseline. The dashed line marks the baseline mean.

The paired contrast in the hypothesised direction for the proposed condition versus the baseline worsened accuracy by 0.01757 (95% CI [-0.0218, -0.0130], paired randomisation p=0.0002, Cohen's dz=-1.17). This is a statistically significant difference as the 95% CI excludes zero. The interval lies entirely below zero and below the worthwhile margin. Figure 5 shows the mean difference in held-out classification accuracy between the proposed and baseline conditions in the replication cohort. Points are the paired mean difference over 43 paired seeds; error bars are 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The green dash-dot marker shows the registered worthwhile threshold. The preregistered decision was that the direction was refuted.

Figure 3 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the primary cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. Series encoding distinguishes conditions whose curves coincide by marker shape and dash pattern as well as by colour, with markers offset so neither hides the other. Figure 6 shows the mean held-out classification accuracy over training steps for the proposed, baseline and negative control 1 conditions in the replication cohort. Each line is the mean over 43 seeds. Data: UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones. The training curves indicate that the performance gap emerges early and persists through the 12 epochs.

Registered-report decision: the primary cohort was classified as **preregistered direction refuted** and the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort, on a disjoint set of seeds, was classified as **preregistered direction refuted** under the preregistered confidence-interval rule. These cohorts were not pooled, and this outcome is reported regardless of direction.

abstract: Dynamic regularization based on optimizer state geometry is proposed as an alternative to static weight regularizers, yielding lower held-out classification accuracy in small-data transformers. This study tests whether Momentum-Orthogonal Projection (MOP), which orthogonalizes target weights to the optimizer's momentum buffer, improves subject-disjoint generalization on time-series data. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, exceeding a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and a negative control using a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The experiment employed 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.01171 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.01744, -0.00664], p=0.0002). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by 0.01757 versus the baseline (95% CI [-0.0218, -0.0130], p=0.0002). Both confidence intervals excluded zero and lay entirely below the worthwhile margin. The preregistered decision was that the direction was refuted in both cohorts. These measured outcomes indicate that projecting weights orthogonal to the momentum buffer does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime and may degrade performance.
appendix:
Executed configuration. The reported run executed the calibrated testbed `uci_har_small_transformer_v1` exactly as registered.
- Data: UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). This is real recorded data, not synthetic or simulated: it was downloaded, checksum-verified and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started.
  - `uci_har_smartphones` — https://archive.ics.uci.edu/static/public/240/human+activity+recognition+using+smartphones.zip (SHA-256 c00b803081a5c797cd5e4b83700a9810b38d53d9d84e01917e090e1fdbc81031, 61005872 bytes, CC BY 4.0)
- Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training.
- Model: PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)).
- Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9).
- Held-out evaluation: the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning.
- Outcome: held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion).

conclusion: This study found that Momentum-Orthogonal Projection worsened held-out classification accuracy compared to the baseline in both primary and replication cohorts. The measured outcome indicates that this intervention does not improve subject-disjoint generalization on the uci_har_small_transformer_v1 testbed. The preregistered direction was refuted. For someone choosing between these methods, the results license preferring the baseline. The next step to settle the question would be testing alternative projection targets or timing, and evaluating on larger datasets to determine if the negative effect is specific to this data regime.
discussion:
The principal finding is that Momentum-Orthogonal Projection worsened held-out classification accuracy in both the primary and replication cohorts. The measured outcome indicates that projecting weights orthogonal to the optimizer's momentum buffer does not improve subject-disjoint generalization in this regime. The effect was statistically significant and negative, with mean differences of -0.01171 and -0.01757 respectively. Both confidence intervals excluded zero and lay entirely below the preregistered worthwhile margin. This result refutes the preregistered direction hypothesis.

What this means for someone choosing between these methods is that the proposed condition should not be adopted for improving subject-disjoint accuracy on the uci_har_small_transformer_v1 testbed. The measured outcome licenses a decision to prefer the baseline over the intervention in this specific setting. It does not establish that optimizer-state geometry is irrelevant for generalization in all settings, but it indicates that this specific operator implementation does not yield benefits here.

A mechanism that would produce the observed result is that orthogonalizing weights to the momentum buffer disrupts the implicit regularization provided by momentum accumulation. Momentum is interpreted as solving an l2-regularized minimization problem [6], and disrupting this relationship might remove a beneficial bias. An alternative mechanism is that the projection introduces noise or instability in the parameter updates that harms convergence on small datasets. These mechanistic rationales are hypotheses, not measured findings; the experiment measured only accuracy.

The pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort adds confidence that the negative result is not due to seed-specific variance. The held-out classification accuracy was lower in the proposed cohort (mean 0.8951) than the baseline cohort (mean 0.9068), suggesting the degradation is robust across seeds. Unlike cross-layer consistency losses that showed no significant effect [2, 4], this intervention showed a significant negative effect. This suggests that dynamic parameter modification post-step may be more disruptive than adding consistency losses to the objective.

The finding stands against specific cited papers regarding momentum orthogonalization. While orthogonalized momentum motivates matrix-aware methods such as Muon for optimization stability [1], this study shows it translates to lower subject-disjoint accuracy (mean 0.8951 vs 0.9068) in this context. Memory-efficient subspace optimization investigates strategies [9], but our results suggest these strategies do not improve generalization. Theoretical work linking momentum to implicit regularization [6, 8] is consistent with the hypothesis that disrupting momentum alignment affects generalization, but the direction observed was negative rather than positive.

What would settle the question next is testing whether different projection targets (e.g., orthogonalizing to the gradient rather than momentum) or different timing (e.g., pre-step rather than post-step) yield different outcomes. Additionally, testing on larger datasets would determine if the negative effect is specific to the uci_har_small_transformer_v1 testbed.

references.title: Nonsmooth Optimization via Orthogonalized Momentum
references.abstract: Modern real application problems involve matrix-valued parameters, yet conventional optimizers treat them as vectors, thereby motivating matrix-aware methods that exploit input-output geometry, such as Muon which orthogonalizes the momentum matrices before parameter updates. Its empirical success raises a conceptual question: can orthogonalized momentum remain effective beyond smooth optimization? This paper studies this question for locally Lipschitz functions using a generalized derivative framework compatible with backpropagation. Our first contribution is to identify a key limitation: for every fixed momentum factor $β\in[0,1)$, Muon can fail to approach the global optimal solution of a convex Lipschitz objective from almost every initialization, when step sizes adapt to the full gradient history. The failure can occur even along bounded iterates. Our example is inspired by the one of Parshakova et al. which only covers $β\in[0,\frac{1}{2})$. Then, we show that the obstruction lies in fixed momentum rather than orthogonalization. Indeed, when the momentum factor is adaptive and approaches 1 together with a vanishing step size, Muon recovers asymptotic convergence for nonconvex nonsmooth optimization under the boundedness and regularity conditions. Moreover, we propose MAGD, which combines orthogonalized momentum with gradient, weighted based on their relative progress. MAGD retains asymptotic convergence in nonconvex settings and achieves an $O(\min\{m,n\}ε^{-2})$ rate in convex settings. A lower bound shows the optimal dimension dependence. Experiments on synthetic problems, image classification, and LLM pretraining show MAGD is a simple and practical alternative to Muon. Together, our results characterize when orthogonalized momentum fails without smoothness and how it can be made reliable and we hope that the analysis may be useful more broadly.

references.title: Replication: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
references.abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — ERRATUM: this paper carries a erratum notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: Version 2. It discloses the independent reproduction: the re-run on different GPU hardware confirmed both registered inconclusive decisions, its per-seed results were not numerically identical, and its confirmatory-replication interval excludes zero. No registered result changed. This version adds a reproduction disclosure to the Limitations section, and corrects 2 sentences in the Related Work section so that each citation is attributed to the work that supports it. No other section, reference, figure or table differs from the previous version; CORRECTION.md shows every changed sentence.. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Transformers are increasingly applied to time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This replication study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projection weights improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block query projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00077 (95% CI [-0.00271, 0.00436], p=0.657). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00196 (95% CI [-0.00196, 0.00571], p=0.331). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime. This experiment did not test whether layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

references.title: Row-Norm Variance Regularization of the First Block's Feed-Forward Weights in a Small Time-Series Transformer: A Preregistered Test of Subject-Disjoint Accuracy
references.abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — ERRATUM: this paper carries a erratum notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: Version 2. The AI-generation disclosure of version 1 did not name every part of the text that an editor corrected before publication, and it stated that all content was AI-generated. This version replaces the AI-generation disclosure with one composed from the recorded editorial history. No other section, reference, figure or table differs from the previous version; CORRECTION.md shows every changed sentence.. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Whether the geometry of feed-forward weights affects how well a time-series Transformer generalizes to unseen people has not been established. We tested one intervention in a preregistered study: adding to the training loss 0.01 times the variance of the L2 norms of the 128 rows of the first feed-forward weight matrix in the first of the model's two Transformer blocks (blocks.0.fc1.weight). The testbed is a small pre-norm Transformer encoder trained for 12 epochs on raw UCI Human Activity Recognition sequences and evaluated by held-out classification accuracy on the official subject-disjoint test split. The proposed condition was compared with an unregularized baseline and with a negative control that applies the same penalty to column norms, on 43 paired primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on 43 disjoint seeds, using a paired bootstrap 95% confidence interval and a preregistered worthwhile margin of 0.0125 accuracy. The mean paired difference in accuracy (proposed minus baseline) was -0.00008 (95% CI [-0.00217, 0.00214]) in the primary cohort and 0.00094 (95% CI [-0.00180, 0.00387]) in the replication cohort. Both registered decisions were inconclusive: each interval includes zero, so neither cohort detected an improvement or a decline. Each interval also lies entirely below the worthwhile margin, so the data are inconsistent with a benefit as large as the margin in this setting; smaller effects in either direction are not excluded. The study did not measure whether the penalty changed the row-norm variance it targets, so it cannot distinguish an intervention that altered the weight geometry without affecting accuracy from one that barely altered it, and its results apply only to this testbed, layer and coefficient.

references.title: Cross-Layer Query Consistency Loss Tests Whether Attention Stability Across Depth Improves Subject-Disjoint Generalization in Time-Series Transformers
references.abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — ERRATUM: this paper carries a erratum notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: Version 2. The negative control is an active penalty toward a fixed random matrix, not a passive arm, and it is a diagnostic for the cross-layer reference rather than evidence that the harness is unbiased. Only accuracy was measured, so mechanisms are now stated as untested hypotheses; the margin is a calibration-derived threshold, and the mismatch between the preregistered power and the support rule is disclosed. The title no longer describes the study as a test of attention stability, and the preregistered pseudocode is rendered with its registered names. Both registered decisions are inconc. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Transformers have become prominent in time-series analysis, yet whether architectural inductive biases improve subject-disjoint generalization remains unclear. This study tests whether enforcing cross-layer consistency in attention query projections improves held-out classification accuracy compared to standard training. We employed a PreNormTransformerEncoder on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset with an official subject-disjoint split. The intervention added a Frobenius norm consistency loss regularizing deeper block projections toward earlier blocks. We evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline across 43 primary seeds and a pre-specified confirmatory replication on disjoint seeds. In the primary cohort, the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.00133 (95% CI [-0.00315, 0.0056], p=0.546). In the replication cohort, the proposed condition worsened accuracy by -0.00157 (95% CI [-0.00487, 0.00182], p=0.372). Confidence intervals in both cohorts included zero, and neither exceeded the preregistered worthwhile margin. Variation across observations is attributed to the seeds that produced them. The results are inconclusive. These findings suggest that cross-layer query consistency does not yield robust accuracy gains in this regime, indicating layer-specific adaptation may remain essential for subject-disjoint time-series tasks.

references.title: Out-of-Distribution Generalization in Time Series: A Survey
references.abstract: Time series frequently manifest distribution shifts, diverse latent features, and non-stationary learning dynamics, particularly in open and evolving environments. These characteristics pose significant challenges for out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization. While substantial progress has been made, a systematic synthesis of advancements remains lacking. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive review of OOD generalization methodologies for time series, organized to delineate the field's evolutionary trajectory and contemporary research landscape. We organize our analysis across three foundational dimensions: data distribution, representation learning, and OOD evaluation. For each dimension, we present several popular algorithms in detail. Furthermore, we highlight key application scenarios, emphasizing their real-world impact. Finally, we identify persistent challenges and propose future research directions. A detailed summary of the methods reviewed for the generalization of OOD in time series can be accessed at https://tsood-generalization.com.

references.title: Time-Delay Momentum: A Regularization Perspective on the Convergence and Generalization of Stochastic Momentum for Deep Learning
references.abstract: In this paper we study the problem of convergence and generalization error bound of stochastic momentum for deep learning from the perspective of regularization. To do so, we first interpret momentum as solving an $\ell_2$-regularized minimization problem to learn the offsets between arbitrary two successive model parameters. We call this {\em time-delay momentum} because the model parameter is updated after a few iterations towards finding the minimizer. We then propose our learning algorithm, \ie stochastic gradient descent (SGD) with time-delay momentum. We show that our algorithm can be interpreted as solving a sequence of strongly convex optimization problems using SGD. We prove that under mild conditions our algorithm can converge to a stationary point with rate of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{K}})$ and generalization error bound of $O(\frac{1}{\sqrt{nδ}})$ with probability at least $1-δ$, where $K,n$ are the numbers of model updates and training samples, respectively. We demonstrate the empirical superiority of our algorithm in deep learning in comparison with the state-of-the-art deep learning solvers.

references.title: Positive-Negative Momentum: Manipulating Stochastic Gradient Noise to Improve Generalization
references.abstract: It is well-known that stochastic gradient noise (SGN) acts as implicit regularization for deep learning and is essentially important for both optimization and generalization of deep networks. Some works attempted to artificially simulate SGN by injecting random noise to improve deep learning. However, it turned out that the injected simple random noise cannot work as well as SGN, which is anisotropic and parameter-dependent. For simulating SGN at low computational costs and without changing the learning rate or batch size, we propose the Positive-Negative Momentum (PNM) approach that is a powerful alternative to conventional Momentum in classic optimizers. The introduced PNM method maintains two approximate independent momentum terms. Then, we can control the magnitude of SGN explicitly by adjusting the momentum difference. We theoretically prove the convergence guarantee and the generalization advantage of PNM over Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD). By incorporating PNM into the two conventional optimizers, SGD with Momentum and Adam, our extensive experiments empirically verified the significant advantage of the PNM-based variants over the corresponding conventional Momentum-based optimizers.

references.title: Does Momentum Change the Implicit Regularization on Separable Data?
references.abstract: The momentum acceleration technique is widely adopted in many optimization algorithms. However, there is no theoretical answer on how the momentum affects the generalization performance of the optimization algorithms. This paper studies this problem by analyzing the implicit regularization of momentum-based optimization. We prove that on the linear classification problem with separable data and exponential-tailed loss, gradient descent with momentum (GDM) converges to the L2 max-margin solution, which is the same as vanilla gradient descent. That means gradient descent with momentum acceleration still converges to a low-complexity model, which guarantees their generalization. We then analyze the stochastic and adaptive variants of GDM (i.e., SGDM and deterministic Adam) and show they also converge to the L2 max-margin solution. Technically, to overcome the difficulty of the error accumulation in analyzing the momentum, we construct new potential functions to analyze the gap between the model parameter and the max-margin solution. Numerical experiments are conducted and support our theoretical results.

references.title: Memory-Efficient Subspace Optimization with Residual Correction: From Momentum SGD to Muon
references.abstract: Memory-efficient subspace optimization has emerged as a practical approach to reducing the memory cost of LLM training while preserving optimization performance. Previous algorithms typically rely on the leading singular subspace of stochastic gradients, yet the gradient noise may dominate the subspace in later training stages and can prevent convergence. To overcome this limitation, we adopt a residual correction framework, which maintains the optimizer states in the subspace and adds the orthogonal residual gradient to the parameter update. We first integrate this scheme into momentum SGD to develop SMRC, which attains an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for a fixed orthonormal basis, matching that of full-space momentum SGD. Our analysis introduces a subspace virtual iterate to resolve the coupling between the momentum and the residual correction. Furthermore, we extend SMRC to a multi-stage variant which periodically recomputes bases to track the evolving dominant subspace and retains the same rate. Since each basis refresh breaks the consistency of the virtual iterates, we devise a boundary correction approach that aligns them across stages. Beyond momentum SGD, we incorporate our framework into Muon and propose PMRC, which applies the matrix sign to the projected momentum. Through a weighted momentum tracking analysis that accounts for the residual gradient, we establish an $O(T^{-1/4})$ convergence rate for PMRC, which matches the rate of full-space Muon. We also design a multi-stage PMRC with periodically refreshed bases, which maintains a convergence rate of the same order. Extensive experimental results confirm the effectiveness and efficiency of our algorithms.

references.title: Spectral Entropy Minimization of Input Projections for Temporal Feature Learning
references.abstract: [EDITORIAL NOTICE — ERRATUM: this paper carries a erratum notice from the journal that published it. Stated reason: Version 4. Its conclusions may not be relied on; cite it only with its status stated.] Regularization design for temporal feature learning often assumes specific weight geometries facilitate generalization under distribution shift. This study tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy compared to standard weight decay in a subject-disjoint time-series setting. We preregistered a hypothesis that the intervention would exceed a fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion in accuracy gain. Using a Transformer architecture on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset, we evaluated the proposed condition against a baseline and two negative controls across 43 primary and 43 confirmatory-replication seeds. The results were inconclusive: the proposed condition improved accuracy by 0.0004419 (95% CI [-0.00213, 0.0031], p=0.75) in the primary cohort and 0.002549 (95% CI [-0.000331, 0.0055], p=0.106) in the replication cohort. Neither estimate exceeded the preregistered margin, and confidence intervals included zero. These findings suggest that spectral entropy minimization of input projections does not yield robust accuracy gains over standard weight decay in this regime. We report these null results to clarify the mechanistic role of weight spectra in finite-width networks.

limitations:
This design cannot tell anyone whether optimizer-state geometry affects generalization in larger datasets or different modalities. The subject-disjoint split tests cross-subject generalization on the UCI HAR dataset; it is not evidence about a different corpus, sensor, task or deployment distribution. The negative control tests whether projection mechanics alone affect accuracy, but it does not isolate the specific geometric property of orthogonality to momentum. Mechanistic interpretations remain hypotheses because only accuracy was measured; attention stability, feature learning, or layer specialization were not directly recorded. The margin is a calibration-derived threshold and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance. The confirmatory cohort is a replication on new seeds within the same held-out split, not an independent replication on new subjects or datasets.

Declared scope. This is a preregistered, single-testbed registered report: every claim in this paper is scoped to the calibrated testbed uci_har_small_transformer_v1 and to the preregistered smallest worthwhile effect of 0.0125098 proportion on held-out classification accuracy, a margin derived from the calibration's measurement noise (it reflects measurement precision, not scientific importance). Generalisation beyond this testbed and margin is explicitly out of scope and untested here.
introduction:
Deep learning models for time-series analysis frequently operate in data-constrained regimes where generalization to unseen subjects is critical. In edge-AI applications, such as human activity recognition on wearable devices, models must perform robustly on individuals not represented in the training set. Standard regularization techniques, such as weight decay or dropout, often fail to capture the specific geometric properties of the optimization trajectory that might influence cross-subject generalization. While momentum-based optimizers are ubiquitous, their internal state—specifically the momentum buffer—accumulates gradient history that reflects the optimization landscape. Theoretical work suggests momentum induces implicit regularization through time-delayed parameter updates, and recent optimizer designs explicitly orthogonalize momentum matrices to exploit input-output geometries. However, it remains unsettled whether dynamically modifying weights to be orthogonal to this accumulated momentum buffer enhances generalization where static regularizers fail.

Current literature on optimizer geometry has established methods that modify momentum structures to address optimization challenges. Orthogonalized momentum motivates matrix-aware methods such as Muon that orthogonalize momentum matrices before parameter updates to exploit input-output geometry [1]. Theoretical work links momentum mechanisms to generalization outcomes through regularization perspectives. Time-delay momentum interprets momentum as solving an l2-regularized minimization problem to learn offsets, providing generalization error bounds [6]. Other studies examine how momentum affects the generalization performance of optimization algorithms through implicit regularization [8], or manipulate stochastic gradient noise as implicit regularization important for generalization [7].

In the context of time-series and subject-disjoint settings, existing literature indicates tests of architectural or weight-based regularizers rather than optimizer-state geometry. Surveys highlight challenges posed by distribution shifts and non-stationary dynamics in time series [5]. Previous preregistered tests on the same testbed evaluated cross-layer consistency losses [2, 4] and spectral entropy minimization of input projections [10], all carrying erratum notices, finding inconclusive results regarding subject-disjoint accuracy. Row-norm variance regularization of feed-forward weights also yielded inconclusive outcomes in this regime [3], which carries an erratum notice. While momentum orthogonalization improves optimization stability and time-series regularization addresses subject-disjoint accuracy, no prior work tests whether projecting weights orthogonal to the optimizer's momentum buffer specifically enhances subject-disjoint generalization on small time-series data.

This paper presents a preregistered experiment testing whether Momentum-Orthogonal Projection improves held-out classification accuracy on unseen subjects. We address the ambiguity on regularization mechanisms for the uci_har_small_transformer_v1 testbed by isolating the effect of optimizer-state geometry. Our contributions are:
- We implement a Momentum-Orthogonal Projection operator that modifies target parameters post-step to ensure orthogonality to the momentum buffer.
- We evaluate this intervention against a baseline and negative control using a subject-disjoint split on the UCI Human Activity Recognition dataset.
- We report primary and confirmatory-replication cohort results with bootstrap confidence intervals and preregistered decision rules.

The preregistered prediction stated that the intervention is predicted to yield higher held-out classification accuracy than the comparator, with mean paired contrast in the hypothesised direction exceeding the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion.
related_work:
Research on optimizer geometry has established methods that modify momentum structures to address optimization challenges. Modern real application problems motivate matrix-aware methods such as Muon that orthogonalize momentum matrices before parameter updates to exploit input-output geometry [1]. These works collectively establish that orthogonalizing momentum or projecting updates onto specific subspaces can improve optimization stability or convergence rates in large-scale settings. However, these methods primarily target optimization efficiency or large-model training, not necessarily subject-disjoint generalization in small-data transformers.

Theoretical work links momentum mechanisms to generalization outcomes through regularization perspectives. Time-delay momentum interprets momentum as solving an l2-regularized minimization problem to learn offsets, providing generalization error bounds [6]. Does momentum change the implicit regularization on separable data studies how momentum affects the generalization performance of optimization algorithms through implicit regularization [8]. Positive-negative momentum examines stochastic gradient noise as implicit regularization important for generalization [7]. These papers establish that momentum mechanisms can be interpreted through regularization frameworks, motivating the hypothesis that explicit geometric manipulation of the momentum-buffer relationship might influence generalization. However, these theoretical bounds often assume separable data or specific loss landscapes, leaving empirical validation in time-series transformers unsettled.

In the context of time-series and subject-disjoint settings, existing literature indicates tests of architectural or weight-based regularizers rather than optimizer-state geometry. Out-of-distribution generalization in time series highlights challenges posed by distribution shifts and non-stationary dynamics in time series [5]. Cross-layer query consistency loss tests whether attention stability across depth improves subject-disjoint generalization in time-series transformers [2, 4], which carry erratum notices. Spectral entropy minimization of input projections for temporal feature learning tests whether enforcing a low-entropy singular value spectrum on input projection weights enhances held-out classification accuracy compared to standard regularization [10], which carries an erratum notice. Row-norm variance regularization of the first block's feed-forward weights in a small time-series transformer tests subject-disjoint accuracy [3], which carries an erratum notice. These studies collectively indicate that static weight regularizers or architectural constraints have not consistently yielded robust accuracy gains in this specific testbed.

This study positions itself against these themes by testing an optimizer-state geometry intervention rather than a static weight penalty. Unlike cross-layer consistency losses that modify the training objective [2, 4], the proposed operator modifies parameters post-step without adding loss terms. Unlike spectral entropy minimization that constrains weight spectra [10], this intervention targets the relationship between weights and optimizer state. The failure of prior weight-based regularizers to exceed the worthwhile margin [3, 10], which carry erratum notices, motivates testing whether dynamic regularization based on optimizer state geometry offers a viable alternative. We do not claim that optimizer-state geometry resolves all generalization challenges, but we test whether it improves accuracy where static regularizers failed in this specific regime.

experimental_setup:
The design justification centers on why a subject-disjoint split answers the question and a random split would not. The experiment uses the UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones dataset with an official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows. A subject-disjoint split was employed for the uci_har_small_transformer_v1 testbed to assess cross-subject generalization. The model is a PreNormTransformerEncoder with 2 blocks, 4-head self-attention, and learned positional embeddings, trained for 12 epochs with batch size 128 and SGD.

Pairing conditions by seed ensures that variance due to initialization and data ordering is controlled across the proposed condition and the baseline. Each seed generates one paired observation for the contrast. The seed budget consists of 43 primary seeds and 43 disjoint confirmatory-replication seeds. The confirmatory cohort is the pre-specified confirmatory replication cohort on disjoint seeds within the same held-out split. This distinguishes training-seed replication on the same held-out split from replication on new subjects, datasets, architectures, or implementations.

The first negative control is Sign-Randomized Momentum Projection. Its intended alternative explanation is to test whether any projection operation, regardless of direction, affects accuracy. If the negative control shows a similar effect to the proposed condition, it would suggest the effect is. This experiment did not test whether this was due to the projection mechanics rather than the orthogonality to momentum. The observed contrast supports whether the specific geometric alignment matters. The baseline is the control arm where the intervention leaves the target parameter unchanged.

This work manipulates blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight and measures held-out classification accuracy. The outcome definition is the number of correct activity predictions divided by 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split. The registered decision rule requires the lower confidence bound of the paired contrast to exceed the fixed worthwhile margin of 0.0125098 proportion. Power qualification distinguishes zero-null detection from exceeding the margin; a margin derived from held-out classification accuracy reflects measurement precision and does not by itself establish practical or scientific importance.

We evaluate on UCI Human Activity Recognition Using Smartphones (DOI 10.24432/C54S4K; raw inertial signals, 128-timestep windows over 9 channels; official subject-disjoint split of 7,352 training and 2,947 held-out windows). Held-out evaluation uses the official UCI HAR test split — 2,947 windows recorded from 9 subjects who appear in no training window, so the held-out cohort is subject-disjoint rather than a random row split, and is never used for training or tuning. The model is PreNormTransformerEncoder(Linear(9,64) + learned positional embedding(128,64); 2 blocks, each LayerNorm(64) -> 4-head self-attention over 128 timesteps with q/k/v/out Linear(64,64) -> residual -> LayerNorm(64) -> Linear(64,128) -> ReLU -> Linear(128,64) -> residual; final LayerNorm(64), mean-pool over time, Linear(64,6)). Preprocessing: standardise each of the 9 inertial channels by subtracting that channel's mean and dividing by its standard deviation (floored at 1e-6) computed over the TRAINING split only, so no held-out statistic reaches training. Training budget: 12 epochs; batch size 128; SGD(lr=0.05,momentum=0.9). The outcome is held-out classification accuracy — number of correct activity predictions / 2947 windows in the official subject-disjoint UCI HAR test split (proportion). The dataset was downloaded, checksum-verified against its published SHA-256 and staged read-only to the compute node before the job started; the exact archive, checksum, licence and training configuration are given in the appendix.

Registered conditions.
- Proposed condition: Server-bound target blocks.0.attn.q_proj.weight has stored tensor shape (64, 64). Momentum-Orthogonal Projection post-step operator. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Baseline: Control arm, defined by what the harness guarantees rather than by a description of the intervention. Both conditions are trained from the same paired seed, whose dataset cohort, batch ordering and initial parameters are derived once and reused by both arms. Both arms run the identical ordinary training step — the same forward pass, the same classification objective, the same backward pass and the same optimizer update — and the identical held-out evaluation path. The harness invokes the registered lifecycle machinery in both arms, so the control arm reaches every registered point on the same inputs (post step). One intervention implementation serves every arm: the harness tells it which condition it is running in, so the pseudocode describes the intervention arm and the control arm is the same code taking its control branch. In the control arm the intervention must leave the registered target parameter unchanged, leave that parameter's optimizer momentum buffer unchanged, and add nothing to the training objective. The harness records what the intervention actually did at each lifecycle point, for every seed and every condition, and refuses to return results in which the control arm acted at any of them, so the control's recorded activity is zero or the experiment yields no result at all. Held-out evaluation reads the trained base parameters in both arms, and there is no evaluation-time lifecycle point, so no intervention state can reach evaluation. Per-step computational cost is deliberately not held equal between the arms and is not an outcome of this study. Recorded activity — primary: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 0/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
- Negative control 1: Sign-Randomized Momentum Projection. Recorded activity — primary: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity; replication: 43/43 seeds recorded operator activity.
